h1:
Sisaket Volcanic Durian Trip
Kantharalak & Khun Han, June–July
intro: Sisaket's volcanic durian comes around just once a year, from mid-June to early July, and the truest way to taste it is to go straight to the orchard — picked ripe off the tree and eaten fresh. So this trip is built as a 2-day, 1-night run focused on the orchards of Kantharalak and Khun Han, one zone per day so you're not driving in circles, tasting in the orchards, sitting in orchard cafes, and tying in local sights and food along the way — with timings, farm-gate prices we checked, this year's festival dates, and an honest heads-up on what to confirm before you go.

blocks.html: This plan starts where most people do: you arrive in Sisaket in the late morning, spend day one in the Kantharalak zone first (lots of orchards and a few orchard cafes where you can sit and eat in comfort), then shift to Khun Han on day two, where Phran sub-district is the densest cluster of durian orchards — grab your gifts to take home, then head back. Each day stays in one district because the drive between Kantharalak and Khun Han runs close to an hour; crisscross between them all day and you'll wear yourself out and not eat durian at your own pace. This trip works best with your own car or a rental, since the orchards sit outside town and public transport barely reaches them.

blocks.title: Check before you set off
blocks.html: Durian is a product of nature — it differs year to year. Before driving a long way, call or message the orchard on Facebook/LINE to ask whether they have fruit right now and whether they're open for tasting in the orchard, because early in the season fruit is scarce and pricey, and some orchards aren't open yet; late in the season some close early once they sell out. This year the Kantharalak District Fruit Festival runs 12–21 June and the main Sisaket Volcanic Durian Festival runs 25–29 June at the field in front of the provincial hall — line up your dates with the festival and you'll find orchards gathered in one place.

blocks.text: When to go to catch the orchards in full fruit

blocks.html: Sisaket durian ripens noticeably later than the eastern provinces. The main season runs roughly from late May to early July, and the stretch when fruit is most plentiful and the most orchards are open is mid to late June. If the rains come early or late, it can shift either way — so if you're planning ahead, aim for mid-June first, then call the orchards to confirm. That's the safest bet. Early in the season there's little fruit and prices are high, with some orchards not yet open; late in the season prices drop but some sellers run out first.

items: Early season (late May–early June) — scarce fruit, high prices, first of the crop. Good for the impatient who want an early taste, but call to check the orchard is open.
Mid season (mid–late June) — the peak. Plentiful fruit, most orchards open, lines up with the festival, prices starting to ease. The best window for this trip.
Late season (early–mid July) — prices drop further, but fruit starts to thin out. Call ahead to every orchard.

blocks.title: How to get there
blocks.html: From Bangkok, take a Southern Isan train straight to Sisaket station, or a bus from Mo Chit. Flying in, land at Ubon Ratchathani airport and drive about an hour and a half. But the durian orchards are outside town, in Kantharalak and Khun Han, and public transport barely reaches them. For this trip you really want to rent a car and drive, or hire a driver for the day. If you genuinely have no car, go during the in-town festival instead — it's far easier to reach.

blocks.title: Book the activities in your Sisaket trip ahead
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

items.label: Day trips from Sisaket
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Kantharalak zone — taste in the orchard + sit in an orchard cafe

items.activity: Arrive in Sisaket, drop your bags at an in-town hotel, then drive out to Kantharalak district
items.note: It's about 1–1.5 hours from town to Kantharalak. Fill up the tank — gas stations thin out as you get into orchard country.

items.activity: Hit your first orchard, walk among the trees, ask to taste the volcanic durian fresh off the tree
items.note: Always ask to taste before buying. Ask how many days ago it was cut and whether it's really from this orchard. Farm-gate prices right now run about 180–250 THB/kg depending on grade and time of season.

items.activity: Settle into an orchard cafe — eat durian over a cold drink
items.note: Such as Win Ka Va Farmhouse & Cafe, a durian orchard with a cafe built in: walk among the trees, then sit down and eat. It gets busy in season, so message their page to ask about timing first.

items.activity: Lunch at a local restaurant around Kantharalak
items.note: Try regional dishes like laab, koi, or tilapia with sweet sadao fish-sauce dip. Line your stomach before more orchards — eat durian all day and it gets cloying.

items.activity: On to a second Kantharalak orchard — pick fruit to take home or give as gifts
items.note: If you're buying gifts, choose an orchard that grades its fruit and can name the source. Ask for fruit that's mature but not fully ripe so it travels without bruising, then let it finish ripening at home.

items.activity: Head back into Sisaket town, keeping the durian in the car with air circulation
items.note: Don't stash it somewhere airless — durian ripens fast and the smell fills the whole car. At the hotel, split it into bags or boxes that breathe.

items.activity: Dinner in town, wander the evening market, save your energy for Khun Han tomorrow
items.note: The evening market and local restaurants in town are full of regional food — som tam, laab, grilled meats with sticky rice.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Khun Han zone — Phran sub-district, the dense orchard belt + gifts

items.activity: Leave town, drive south to Khun Han district, heading for Phran sub-district
items.note: About 1–1.5 hours from town. Phran is the densest belt of volcanic durian orchards in Khun Han, and as you head south the scenery turns to forested hills at the foot of the Phanom Dong Rak range.

items.activity: Visit the orchards around Phran, taste and grade
items.note: Around here you get both big graded orchards and small family farms. Many owners walk you through the trees and tell you about the volcanic soil. Ask to taste first — you can compare several orchards since they're close together.

items.activity: On to another orchard, pick premium fruit for gifts
items.note: If you're buying a lot, choose an orchard that clearly separates grades and tells you what you get for what you pay. Premium grade runs about 250 THB/kg, quality grade about 200 THB/kg — there's room to bargain if you buy several kilos.
Local restaurants in the district town serve laab, koi, soups, and bold Sisaket-style tam, priced from tens to low hundreds of baht a plate. Refuel before moving on.

items.activity: Stop at the Million Bottle Temple (Wat Pa Maha Chedi Kaew) if you still have the energy
items.note: It's in Khun Han, with the whole temple decorated in over 1.5 million glass bottles. The highlight is the four-gabled ubosot set over water. Open roughly 08:00–17:00, free entry, dress modestly in the ubosot area — a little break from durian.

items.activity: Grab gifts before heading back — your last durian + seasonal volcanic fruit
items.note: The same season brings volcanic rambutan and mangosteen too, grown on the same soil. You can also pick up Thung Kula jasmine rice or hang rice as extra gifts.
If you're taking the train back, check times ahead — evenings get busy. Flying out of Ubon Ratchathani, allow about 1.5 hours' drive to the airport. Keep the durian ventilated the whole way.

blocks.text: Orchards open for tasting, where people actually go

blocks.html: Below are the orchards and volcanic durian buying spots people actually visit in Kantharalak, Si Rattana, and Khun Han. Some are orchards open for a walk-through with a cafe to sit and eat in; some are farmers' storefronts selling fresh-cut fruit. Prices are approximate ranges, depending on grade and time of season — high early, easing in the middle. Call or message every one before you go, because fruit sells out fast.

items.name: Win Ka Va Farmhouse & Cafe
items.blurb: A Kantharalak volcanic durian orchard that doubles as an orchard cafe — walk among the trees and sit down to eat fresh durian over a drink, all in one place. Great if you want the real orchard atmosphere rather than just buying to take home. It's the first pin I'd recommend on day one of this plan.

items.name: Salete Labeur Orchard
items.blurb: A volcanic durian orchard that sells right at the farm gate — reviewers drop by often. Cut fresh from the tree, pick your own fruit, with a genuine family-orchard feel. Good to stop at while touring Kantharalak–Si Rattana.

items.name: Wanarak Orchard
items.blurb: A Kantharalak orchard selling direct from the farm, with volcanic Monthong at more reachable prices than many. Focused on properly tree-ripened fruit. If you want durian to actually eat rather than to photograph, this one's good value.

items.name: Mae Si Chan Volcanic Durian Orchard
items.blurb: A Kantharalak orchard with both volcanic durian and volcanic rambutan, selling at the farm gate in season. Handy for picking up several things at once — the rambutan here is grown on the same volcanic soil.

items.name: Volcanic Soil Durian, Ban Sam Khilek
items.blurb: An orchard around Ban Sam Khilek in Phran sub-district, Khun Han district — one of the densest durian belts in the district. Cut fresh, sold at the farm gate. A good pin for day two of the plan, since it sits in a zone with many orchards clustered together.
items.meta: Khun Han District, Phran sub-district · farm-gate sales

items.name: Lung Soem Orchard
items.blurb: A volcanic durian orchard in Phran sub-district, Khun Han, that local authorities have featured. Cut fresh from the tree, and the owner will walk you through the trees. Great if you like supporting small family orchards and hearing the volcanic-soil story straight from the grower.
items.meta: Khun Han District, Phran sub-district · small family orchard

items.name: Chok Mueang Si Volcanic Durian Orchard
items.blurb: A well-known Khun Han orchard selling fresh-cut, graded fruit. Prices run a bit higher because they keep quality tight. Good if you want handsome fruit with firm flesh you'd be proud to give as a gift.

items.name: Bun Song Orchard
items.blurb: A Khun Han orchard with clearly separated grades — premium and quality at different prices, and they tell you exactly what you get for what you pay. Good if you want to choose by budget. Cut fresh from the orchard.

items.name: Ta Toem Orchard
items.blurb: A small orchard reviewers stop by to taste at often, with a genuine family-orchard feel. The owner walks you through the trees and tells you about the volcanic soil. There isn't much fruit, so go when it's in season to find any.

items.name: Roadside stalls along the Khun Han–Kantharalak route
items.blurb: In season, farmers set up stalls along the main roads in and out of the growing area. Prices are negotiable and the selection is varied, but you need a good eye — choose sellers who can name the orchard source, and ask to taste before you buy.

blocks.title: How to buy without getting burned
blocks.html: Always ask to taste first — durian at just-right ripeness is soft but not mushy, sweet and rich without bitterness. Be wary of any seller who won't let you taste at all. Ask how many days ago it was cut; if you want to eat it that same day, choose fruit that's starting to smell. If you're carrying it far, pick fruit that's mature but not fully ripe and let it finish ripening yourself. Buying at the farm gate usually gets you a better price and a clearer source than buying roadside.

blocks.text: Why eat it at the orchard instead of ordering online

blocks.html: Volcanic durian is mostly the Monthong variety, same as the eastern provinces, but it's grown on old volcanic soil at the foot of the Phanom Dong Rak range — weathered from basalt, sticky red, well-draining, and rich in nutrients. The result is drier flesh, crisp outside and soft within, sweet and rich without being cloying, with a milder smell than usual durian. Plenty of people who normally avoid durian because of the smell can eat this one. Fruit like this you really have to taste at the orchard to understand, because it's cut ripe off the tree and eaten fresh — the flavor isn't the same as buying it and ripening it at home — and you get to see the real trees, talk to the growers, and pick your own fruit too.

items: Dry, firm flesh — not mushy; holds its shape when you scoop it
Sweet and rich without being cloying — just-right sweetness, followed by richness
Milder smell than usual — many people who fear durian's smell can eat this one
Cut ripe off the tree — eaten fresh in the orchard, it tastes different from home-ripened
A GI product — registered to a defined growing area, grown only in Kantharalak, Khun Han, and Si Rattana
Accommodation, 1 night — in-town guesthouses from about 400–700 THB, mid-range hotels 800–1,500 THB
Car — a self-drive rental runs about 1,000–1,500 THB a day, split among the group, plus fuel
Durian — taste as you please; budget around 500–1,500 THB, allow more if you're buying fruit to take home or give as gifts
Food, 2 days — regional food and the evening market run about 400–600 THB for the whole trip
Attraction entry — the Million Bottle Temple and the stops in this plan are free; just parking or a donation if you wish

blocks.text: When is the volcanic durian festival this year

blocks.html: If you'd rather not drive around hunting orchard by orchard, the season has festivals that bring the orchards together in one place. This year there are two main events: the Kantharalak District Fruit Festival, 12–21 June, in front of the Kantharalak district office, and the main Sisaket Volcanic Durian Festival, 25–29 June, at the field in front of the provincial hall. The main event gathers volcanic Monthong durian from orchards across the area, along with rambutan, mangosteen, OTOP products, and local specialties — come on a festival day and you get it all in one go. But if you want the real orchard atmosphere and the taste of fruit cut fresh off the tree, the 2-day orchard run still has more soul. Festival dates shift each year with the season, so always check the province's announcement first.

blocks.title: If you can't make the festival dates
blocks.html: Many orchards ship volcanic durian online direct from the farm — choose a page that clearly names the growing source and has reviews. But once you're already in Sisaket, tasting it fresh in the orchard has more soul any day. Try aiming for mid-June, when fruit is most plentiful.

blocks.text: Pha Mo I Daeng–Preah Vihear, why they're not in this plan

blocks.html: Many people think of Kantharalak alongside Pha Mo I Daeng and the climb up to Preah Vihear, but this durian trip deliberately leaves them out, because Pha Mo I Daeng in Khao Phra Wihan National Park was announced temporarily closed to tourism from 29 May 2025 amid tensions along the Thai–Cambodian border, and it still depends on the situation there. So this plan focuses on the durian orchards, temples, and food in areas you can visit as normal instead.

blocks.title: If you want to add Pha Mo I Daeng
blocks.html: Before planning to go, always check the latest announcements from Khao Phra Wihan National Park and the border situation — don't rely on old information. If it's still closed on your dates, focus on the durian orchards and temples in this plan instead, and you won't waste the trip.

blocks.text: Can you do it as a day trip or 3 days?

blocks.html: Both work. If you're really short on time, cut it to a single zone — pick either Kantharalak or Khun Han, spend half a day tasting at 2–3 orchards and the other half grabbing gifts and the Million Bottle Temple, and you'll get your fill of durian in one day. If you have 3 days, add Si Rattana, which is also a registered GI growing area, and stop at Samrong Kiat Waterfall or the Khmer ruins around the area. The 2-day, 1-night plan, though, hits the sweet spot for anyone who wants both the Kantharalak and Khun Han orchards without rushing.

faq.q: When is the best time to eat Sisaket volcanic durian?
faq.a: The main season is roughly late May to early July, with fruit most plentiful and the most orchards open from mid to late June. Aim for mid-June first, then call the orchards to confirm, since timing shifts each year with the rains. Early in the season there's little fruit and prices are high; late in the season prices drop but fruit starts running out.

faq.q: Do you need your own car for this trip?
faq.a: You really should have one, because the durian orchards are outside town in Kantharalak and Khun Han, and public transport barely reaches them. Rent a car and drive, or hire a driver for the day. If you genuinely have no car, go during the in-town festival instead — it's far easier to reach.

faq.q: How much does volcanic durian cost at the farm gate?
faq.a: It depends on grade and time of season, but generally about 180–250 THB per kilo — premium grade around 250 THB, quality grade around 200 THB. Prices are high early in the season and ease from mid to late season. Buying at the farm gate usually gets you a better price and a clearer source than roadside.

faq.q: When is the Sisaket volcanic durian festival this year?
faq.a: This year there are two main events: the Kantharalak District Fruit Festival, 12–21 June, in front of the Kantharalak district office, and the main Sisaket Volcanic Durian Festival, 25–29 June, at the field in front of the provincial hall, gathering orchards from across the area in one place. Festival dates shift each year with the season, so check the province's announcement before you go.

faq.q: How should you split the days so it's not exhausting?
faq.a: One zone per day. Spend day one in Kantharalak, which has orchards with cafes built in, and day two in Khun Han, especially Phran sub-district, the dense orchard belt. The drive between the two districts runs close to an hour, so crisscrossing all day leaves you worn out and unable to eat durian at your own pace.
